narrative:
The decision to deny your application rests on a prediction that you would have a roughly 51 percent chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is slightly above the point of even odds, the law school judged the risk of admitting you to be too high.

Of the factors the model weighed, your third-year class standing was by far the most influential—and it worked strongly against you. You finished in the second decile of your class, while students who were accepted typically ranked near the sixth decile. This single measure of academic performance outweighed everything else, and it was the clearest reason your application was denied.

Two other factors did help you. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30, which is slightly above the accepted-student average of 3.23, pushed the prediction in your favor, suggesting solid overall academic ability. Your LSAT score of 36, although slightly below the accepted average of 37.18, also nudged toward passing rather than failure—so it was not a cause for concern in your case.

The problem remains that the strong negative signal from your class rank outweighed these positive contributions. What you can do next is address that concern directly: focus on raising your final-year grades or retaking challenging courses to improve your standing. Retaking the LSAT could also help, but improving your academic performance in your last year is the most impactful step. If you can demonstrate stronger class performance, you could reapply next cycle with a much more favorable prediction.
